\section[il disaccordo]{il disaccordo — the disagreement}

\label{lesson:IT-C341-disaccordo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for convincing, then the Italian for to persuade.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: il disaccordo}
\textbf{il disaccordo} — \textquotedblleft{}the disagreement\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Siamo in disaccordo su quasi tutto.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{We disagree about almost everything.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Essere in disaccordo} — to disagree. The opposite is \emph{essere d'accordo}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{disaccordo} is built from \emph{dis-} and \emph{accordo} \textquotedblleft{}agreement\textquotedblright{}, which comes from \emph{accordare}, a verb usually traced to Vulgar Latin \emph{accordāre}, built on Latin \emph{cor, cordis} \textquotedblleft{}heart\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB): hearts that do not beat together.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{il disaccordo}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{il disaccordo}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{il disaccordo}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for convincing, then the Italian for to persuade, then say \emph{il disaccordo} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does il disaccordo mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The disagreement\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[obiettare]{obiettare — to object}

\label{lesson:IT-C341-obiettare}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to persuade, then the Italian for the disagreement.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: obiettare}
\textbf{obiettare} — \textquotedblleft{}to object\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Posso obiettare una cosa? Il prezzo è troppo alto.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{May I object to one thing? The price is too high.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Obiettare che} — to object that. Formal; in speech many people say \emph{non sono d'accordo}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{obiettare} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{obiectāre} \textquotedblleft{}to throw against, to set before, to reproach\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), formed on \emph{obicere}, built from \emph{ob} \textquotedblleft{}against\textquotedblright{} and \emph{iacere} \textquotedblleft{}to throw\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{obiettare}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{obiettare}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{obiettare}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for to persuade, then the Italian for the disagreement, then say \emph{obiettare} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does obiettare mean? (\textquotedblleft{}To object\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[l'obiezione]{l'obiezione — the objection}

\label{lesson:IT-C341-obiezione}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the disagreement, then the Italian for to object.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: l'obiezione}
\textbf{l'obiezione} — \textquotedblleft{}the objection\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Nessuna obiezione? Allora cominciamo.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{No objections? Then let us begin.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Fare un'obiezione} — to raise an objection. \emph{Nessuna obiezione} — no objection.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{obiezione} is a learned borrowing from Late Latin \emph{obiectiō} \textquotedblleft{}a throwing against, an objection\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{obicere} \textquotedblleft{}to throw against\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), built on \emph{iacere} \textquotedblleft{}to throw\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for the disagreement, then the Italian for to object, then say \emph{l'obiezione} again

\section[ribattere]{ribattere — to answer back, to retort}

\label{lesson:IT-C341-ribattere}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for to object, then the Italian for the objection.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ribattere}
\textbf{ribattere} — \textquotedblleft{}to answer back, to retort\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Lei ha subito ribattuto che non era vero.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{She immediately retorted that it was not true.}
\end{quote}

Literally to beat back: you hit the ball back over the net.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{ribattere} is built from \emph{ri-} \textquotedblleft{}back, again\textquotedblright{} and \emph{battere} \textquotedblleft{}to beat\textquotedblright{}, which is inherited from Latin \emph{battuere} \textquotedblleft{}to beat\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{ribattere}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{ribattere}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for to object, then the Italian for the objection, then say \emph{ribattere} again
\end{itemize}

\section[contraddire]{contraddire — to contradict}

\label{lesson:IT-C341-contraddire}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the objection, then the Italian for to answer back.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: contraddire}
\textbf{contraddire} — \textquotedblleft{}to contradict\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Non mi piace quando mi contraddici davanti a tutti.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I do not like it when you contradict me in front of everyone.}
\end{quote}

Conjugated like \emph{dire}: \emph{contraddico, contraddici, contraddice}. \emph{Contraddirsi} is to contradict yourself.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{contraddire} comes from Latin \emph{contrādīcere} \textquotedblleft{}to speak against\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built from \emph{contrā} \textquotedblleft{}against\textquotedblright{} and \emph{dīcere} \textquotedblleft{}to say\textquotedblright{}; Italian reshaped it on \emph{dire}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
